In particular, neoplasms within the spectrum of Sertoliform cystadenoma, given their morphologic and immunophenotypic features, may need to be distinguised from Sertoli cell tumor NOS, metastatic ductal adenocarcinoma of the prostate, and papillary renal cell carcinoma, among others. As shown in this study, the presence of areas of transition between non-neoplastic and neoplastic epithelium within the rete testis can be helpful to support a diagnosis of Sertoliform cystadenoma of the rete testis. Additionally, positivity for PAX8 and absence of nuclear beta-catenin expression are helpful to distinguish between these neoplasms and Sertoli cell tumor NOS. In our opinion, the presence of nuclear beta-catenin expression is so consistent among indolent Sertoli cell tumour NOS that, in its absence, this diagnosis should be restricted to cases with prototypical features. Given that Sertoli cell tumours NOS typically occur within the testis proper, the combination of purely intra-rete growth pattern and the absence of nuclear beta-catenin expression argue against it, even in the presence of SF-1 expression.

map_chunks.summary_text: This chunk introduces benign tumours of the rete testis, which consist predominantly of cystadenomas and adenomas [S1|PMC12129600_HIS-87-35|15493]. A morphologically distinct subset exhibiting tubular or tubulopapillary architecture closely mimics Sertoli cell tumours and was historically designated 'Sertoliform cystadenomas of the rete testis' [S2|PMC12129600_HIS-87-35|15493]. The most recent WHO classification has reclassified these as Sertoli cell tumours NOS with pure intra-rete growth, effectively abolishing them as a standalone entity [S3|PMC12129600_HIS-87-35|15493]. The remaining cystadenomas of the rete testis show a vague morphological resemblance to Müllerian-origin tumours of the ovary [S4|PMC12129600_HIS-87-35|15493]. The study aims to analyse benign rete testis tumours including the Sertoliform subset [S5|PMC12129600_HIS-87-35|15493].

map_chunks.summary_text: This chunk addresses benign tumours of the rete testis and the nosological status of Sertoliform cystadenoma. Benign rete testis tumours are rare and predominantly include cystadenomas and adenomas with papillary or tubulopapillary architecture [S1|PMC12129600_HIS-87-35|15498]. A subset was historically designated "Sertoliform cystadenoma of the rete testis" owing to partial morphologic resemblance to Sertoli cell tumours [S2|PMC12129600_HIS-87-35|15498]. A key distinguishing feature is their pure intra-rete growth pattern, which contrasts with Sertoli cell tumours NOS [S3|PMC12129600_HIS-87-35|15498]. However, the latest WHO classification of urinary and male genital tumours absorbed Sertoliform cystadenomas into Sertoli cell tumours NOS, eliminating them as a separate entity [S4|PMC12129600_HIS-87-35|15498].

map_chunks.summary_text: This introductory chunk establishes the clinical context and study scope for benign rete testis neoplasms. Benign neoplasms of the rete testis—specifically adenomas and Sertoliform cystadenomas—are generally recognizable but may require exclusion of malignant tumours, including metastatic carcinomas from multiple primary sites, which are significantly more frequent [S1|PMC12129600_HIS-87-35|15499]. Crucially, the histopathologic, immunophenotypic, and molecular characteristics of these benign tumours remain largely undescribed in the literature [S2|PMC12129600_HIS-87-35|15499]. To address this gap, the authors present a case series of 11 benign rete testis tumours with comprehensive morphologic, immunophenotypic, and molecular profiling [S3|PMC12129600_HIS-87-35|15499].

This chunk describes the study methodology for a case series investigating benign neoplasms of the rete testis. It covers case identification (institutional and personal consultation files), data collection (clinicopathologic data from medical records and pathology reports including age, clinical presentation, procedure, and tumour size), histological review (H&E-stained slides), and IHC panel application (antibodies per Table 1, with some results sourced from original diagnostic work-up). No generalizable medical facts (demographics, morphology, IHC results, molecular genetics, staging, treatment, or prognosis) are reported in this chunk — only methods are described.

map_chunks.summary_text: This chunk describes the molecular sequencing methodology used for solid tumour genomic profiling. Tumour DNA was manually dissected from FFPE sections [S1|PMC12129600_HIS-87-35|15502], extracted by standard protocols, and sequenced at the University of Bologna Solid Tumour Molecular Pathology Laboratory using three laboratory-developed panels aligned to hg19/GRCh37 [S2|PMC12129600_HIS-87-35|15502]. Approximately 30 ng of DNA per panel was amplified using the AmpliSeq Plus Library Kit 2.0 [S3|PMC12129600_HIS-87-35|15502], sequenced on an Ion S5 Prime instrument, and analysed with Ion Reporter v5.20 [S4|PMC12129600_HIS-87-35|15502]. Variant calling required SNVs/Indels to be present in ≥5% of reads and detected on both strands [S5|PMC12129600_HIS-87-35|15502]; results were reviewed for clinical/biological relevance by a molecular pathology expert [S6|PMC12129600_HIS-87-35|15502].

This chunk describes 4 cases of 'Sertoliform adenoma/cystadenoma' of the rete testis [S1|PMC12129600_HIS-87-35|15504]. Grossly, tumours were solid (1 case) or solid and cystic (3 cases) and well-circumscribed [S2|PMC12129600_HIS-87-35|15504]; 3/4 showed clear confinement within expanded rete testis profiles [S3|PMC12129600_HIS-87-35|15504]. Architecturally, 3 tumours were tubulo-papillary and 1 was tubular-trabecular, all reminiscent of a Sertoli cell lesion [S4|PMC12129600_HIS-87-35|15504]. Tubules were elongated and branching with continuity to papillary structures [S5|PMC12129600_HIS-87-35|15504]; papillae were slender with occasional branching, and one case showed fibrovascular core hyalinization from basement membrane material deposits [S6|PMC12129600_HIS-87-35|15504]. The solid tumour displayed a 'tram-track' trabecular pattern, prominent intratumoral lymphocytes, and occasional hyaline globules [S7–S8|PMC12129600_HIS-87-35|15504]. Cytologically, tumour cells were eosinophilic, cuboidal to columnar with minimal-to-mild atypia; nuclei were oval/elongated/slightly irregular with fine chromatin [S9|PMC12129600_HIS-87-35|15504]. Nucleoli were inconspicuous and mitotic activity was uniformly low (<1/10 HPF) [S10|PMC12129600_HIS-87-35|15504].

This chunk describes morphological and immunohistochemical features of a series of testicular/rete-associated adenomas. Necrosis, invasive growth, and angioinvasion were absent in all tumours [S1|PMC12129600_HIS-87-35|15504]. In 3 of the tumours, transition areas between the flat nonneoplastic rete epithelium and neoplastic adenoma epithelium were clearly identified, arguing against a Sertoli cell origin [S2|PMC12129600_HIS-87-35|15504]. IHC revealed diffuse PAX8 expression in all cases (4/4) [S3|PMC12129600_HIS-87-35|15504]. Beta-catenin expression was confined to the cytoplasmic membrane in all 4 cases, with the sentence truncated before completion regarding nuclear staining [S4|PMC12129600_HIS-87-35|15504].

findings.claim: Benign cystadenoma lining epithelium -> mixture of mucinous and ciliated columnar cells (1/7 tumours)
findings.verbatim_support: The remaining seven tumours were entirely cystic and classified as benign cystadenomas. The lining epithelium contained mucinous cells in two tumours (Figure 4A), a mixture of mucinous and ciliated columnar cells in one tumour (Figure 4B); and cuboidal to short columnar cells in the remaining four tumours. Based on their microscopic appearance, the cysts seemed unilocular/simple (i.e. they lacked internal septations) and were lined by a single layer of epithelial cells. Focal stubby, branching papillae were seen in one neoplasm that did not contain mucinous cells (Figure 5A,B). Some lesions showed inflammatory cells (within the mucin) and/ or evidence of reaction to extravasated mucin. True stratification was not seen, although pseudostratification occurred focally, including in the tumour with stubby papillae. Of note, in the latter, the epithelium lining the papillae showed more significant nuclear atypia, with conspicuous nucleoli, than the remaining neoplasms in this group (Figure 5B). Very focal areas with ovarian-like stroma were seen in only two tumours (Figures 5 and 6). Mitotic activity was consistently low (below one mitotic figure per 10 high-power fields), and necrosis, invasive growth, or lymphovascular invasion were not seen. All lesions were tested de-novo for PAX8, WT1, and CDX2. Immunohistochemistry demonstrated that PAX8 was expressed in scattered cells of 1/7 tumours, WT1 in 2/7 tumours, and CDX2 in 2/7 tumours (Table 2).

map_chunks.summary_text: This chunk describes the histopathological features of seven entirely cystic benign cystadenomas [S1|PMC12129600_HIS-87-35|15506]. The lining epithelium was heterogeneous: mucinous cells in two tumours, a mixed mucinous/ciliated columnar pattern in one, and cuboidal-to-short columnar cells in four [S2|PMC12129600_HIS-87-35|15506]. All cysts appeared unilocular/simple, lacking internal septations, and were lined by a single epithelial layer [S3|PMC12129600_HIS-87-35|15506]. One non-mucinous tumour harboured focal stubby, branching papillae [S4|PMC12129600_HIS-87-35|15506] and displayed greater nuclear atypia with conspicuous nucleoli compared to the remaining group [S7|PMC12129600_HIS-87-35|15506]. Some lesions contained inflammatory cells within mucin and/or evidence of extravasated mucin reaction [S5|PMC12129600_HIS-87-35|15506]. True stratification was universally absent, though focal pseudostratification occurred [S6|PMC12129600_HIS-87-35|15506]. Ovarian-like stroma was seen only focally in two of the seven tumours [S8|PMC12129600_HIS-87-35|15506]. Benign features were consistent: mitotic activity was uniformly low (<1/10 HPF), and necrosis, invasive growth, and lymphovascular invasion were all absent [S9|PMC12129600_HIS-87-35|15506]. All lesions were tested de-novo by IHC for PAX8, WT1, and CDX2 [S10|PMC12129600_HIS-87-35|15506].

findings.claim: Sertoliform cystadenoma of the rete testis (4 lesions) -> negative for pathogenic CTNNB1 variants
findings.verbatim_support: The current WHO classification of urinary and male genital tumours does include a category for adenomas of the rete testis, but there is no explanation of how these tumours differ from those previously described as 'Sertoliform' cystadenomas in the literature. Hence, the interpretation of what constitutes a Sertoli cell tumour NOS with growth confined to the rete testis and a true adenoma of the rete testis seems entirely arbitrary. Moreover, to the best of our knowledge, there is no convincing documentation of a Sertoli cell tumour with pure intra-rete growth. The present study demonstrates that four lesions within the spectrum of Sertoliform cystadenoma of the rete testis (and originally classified as such) were negative for pathogenic CTNNB1 variants, lacked nuclear expression of beta-catenin, and were positive for PAX8. Additionally, three tumours showed a clear transition between the nonneoplastic rete epithelium and the neoplastic epithelium. These findings argue against the possibility of a Sertoli cell tumour NOS growing into the rete testis, especially considering that over 90% of indolent Sertoli cell tumours show CTNNB1 or APC variants and nuclear beta-catenin expression and are negative for PAX8 nuclear expression.

findings.claim: Benign neoplasms of rete testis (excluding Sertoliform cystadenomas) -> entirely cystic architecture
findings.verbatim_support: Unlike Sertoliform cystadenomas, which are solid and cystic or solid, most of the remaining benign neoplasms of the rete testis are entirely cystic. These benign cystadenomas are generally wellcircumscribed, discovered incidentally, and characterized by cystic spaces lined by a single layer of cuboidal to columnar epithelial cells. A subset may contain mucinous epithelium with intraluminal mucin, and some tumours include a subpopulation of ciliated cells. Based on morphologic findings, these tumours have often been interpreted as testicular counterparts of similar-appearing Mullerian tumours of the ovaries, but the immunophenotypic and molecular features of these lesions had not been previously studied in detail. Mucinous or serous ovarian neoplasms may harbour KRAS or BRAF mutations, which were not identified in benign cystadenomas of the rete testis (including a case with focal epithelial proliferation consisting of stubby papillae lined by short columnar cells). An important caveat is that, due to their nature, tumour cellularity is often low in these neoplasms, making the molecular analysis challenging.

map_chunks.summary_text: This chunk characterizes benign cystadenomas of the rete testis in contrast to Sertoliform cystadenomas. Sertoliform cystadenomas have solid and cystic or purely solid architecture [S1], whereas the remaining benign rete testis neoplasms are entirely cystic [S1]. Benign cystadenomas are well-circumscribed, incidentally discovered, and lined by a single layer of cuboidal to columnar epithelium [S2]. A subset harbours mucinous epithelium with intraluminal mucin [S3], and some contain ciliated cells [S3]. Morphologically, these tumours have been likened to ovarian Mullerian neoplasms [S4]; however, unlike mucinous/serous ovarian tumours—which may harbour KRAS or BRAF mutations—these mutations were not identified in benign rete testis cystadenomas, including a case with focal epithelial proliferation showing stubby papillae [S5]. A key technical caveat is that low tumour cellularity in these lesions makes molecular analysis challenging [S6].

findings.claim: Sertoliform cystadenoma of the rete testis requires distinction from Sertoli cell tumour NOS, metastatic ductal adenocarcinoma of the prostate, and papillary renal cell carcinoma due to overlapping morphologic and immunophenotypic features
findings.verbatim_support: From a practical perspective, the distinction between these tumours of the rete testis and metastases, germ cell tumours, or other malignant neoplasms, is seldom problematic, especially when they are entirely cystic. However, tumours with solid components may show significant overlap with sex cord stromal tumours and may occasionally raise the possibility of metastases to the testis. In particular, neoplasms within the spectrum of Sertoliform cystadenoma, given their morphologic and immunophenotypic features, may need to be distinguised from Sertoli cell tumor NOS, metastatic ductal adenocarcinoma of the prostate, and papillary renal cell carcinoma, among others. As shown in this study, the presence of areas of transition between non-neoplastic and neoplastic epithelium within the rete testis can be helpful to support a diagnosis of Sertoliform cystadenoma of the rete testis. Additionally, positivity for PAX8 and absence of nuclear beta-catenin expression are helpful to distinguish between these neoplasms and Sertoli cell tumor NOS. Entirely cystic rete testis tumours are seldom problematic, but those with solid components overlap significantly with sex cord stromal tumours and may raise concern for metastases [S1–S2|PMC12129600_HIS-87-35|15512]. Key diagnostic features for Sertoliform cystadenoma include the presence of transitional areas between non-neoplastic and neoplastic epithelium within the rete testis [S4|PMC12129600_HIS-87-35|15512]. map_chunks.summary_text: This chunk presents two key conclusions from a study of rete testis tumours using sequencing panels. First, benign tumours previously called Sertoliform cystadenomas of the rete testis — recently reclassified by the WHO as Sertoli cell tumours NOS with intra-rete growth — lack the hallmark features of Sertoli cell tumours NOS (apart from tubular/tubulopapillary architecture), suggesting the WHO reclassification is likely incorrect [S2|PMC12129600_HIS-87-35|15513; S3|PMC12129600_HIS-87-35|15513]. Second, cystadenomas of the rete testis do not harbour the molecular alterations characteristic of mucinous Müllerian-origin tumours of the ovary, indicating they are likely not a true counterpart to such neoplasms [S4|PMC12129600_HIS-87-35|15513]. The authors note that sequencing panel limitations precluded identification of novel variants, and further studies are warranted [S5|PMC12129600_HIS-87-35|15513].
